nameStory: Low water-milfoil gets its name from its preference for shallow waters and muddy edges where water levels fluctuate - hence 'low' water conditions. The 'milfoil' part comes from the Latin words 'mille' (thousand) and 'folium' (leaf), referring to the finely divided, feathery leaves that look like they have countless tiny segments. Early botanists thought these delicate, thread-like leaf divisions resembled tiny feathers or the finest embroidery.
description: Low water-milfoil is a small aquatic plant that grows both underwater and along muddy shorelines in shallow areas. Unlike its larger cousins, this milfoil stays relatively short, typically reaching only 4-12 inches tall when growing emersed (above water). The plant has delicate, feathery leaves that are finely divided into thread-like segments, giving it an almost moss-like appearance when viewed from a distance. It forms low mats or patches in areas where water levels change seasonally.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Feathery leaves divided into hair-thin segments that feel soft and flexible when touched underwater, arranged in whorls of 3-6 around the stem like tiny green bottle brushes

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms low, creeping mats in shallow water or muddy shores, much shorter and more compact than other water-milfoils, rarely exceeding 12 inches in height

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny, inconspicuous reddish or greenish flowers appear above water on short spikes, each flower only about 1/8 inch across with 4 petals

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Slender, reddish-brown stems that feel somewhat brittle when handled, often rooting at nodes where they touch mud or sediment

idTips.label: Habitat Preference
idTips.description: Found in areas where water levels fluctuate seasonally, often growing both submerged and emerged, adapting to changing water conditions

habitat: Low water-milfoil thrives in shallow ponds, pond margins, seasonal pools, and muddy areas that experience changing water levels throughout the year. It prefers acidic to neutral waters and can tolerate both fully submerged conditions and temporary exposure when water levels drop. You'll find it in quiet backwaters, shallow coves of larger water bodies, and small woodland pools across New England.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as water warms, with fresh feathery leaves appearing bright green. Plants begin active growth in shallow areas as ice melts.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season with full leaf development and small flower spikes appearing above water surface from June through August. This is the best time for identification when all features are visible.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and plants may take on reddish tints. Growth slows as temperatures cool and some portions may die back if water levels drop.
seasonality.winter: Most above-water portions die back, but underwater parts may persist in milder areas. Plant is largely dormant and difficult to identify during this season.

funFact: Low water-milfoil is like a botanical shape-shifter - when growing underwater, its leaves are finely divided and feathery, but if water levels drop and the same plant finds itself on land, it can produce completely different leaves that are more compact and less divided to prevent water loss!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other water-milfoils, but low water-milfoil is much shorter and grows in shallower conditions. Remember: if you're looking at a tall, robust water-milfoil in deep water, it's probably not this species - low water-milfoil stays 'low' both in stature and water depth preference.
contextualKnowledge: With only 33 recorded observations in New England, low water-milfoil is quite uncommon and may be overlooked due to its small size and preference for temporary or seasonal water bodies that botanists visit less frequently. It's a native species, unlike some of its more common invasive relatives.
compareHints: Low water-milfoil is the shortest member of its genus in New England, staying under a foot tall while Eurasian water-milfoil can reach 10 feet long. Unlike the robust, dense growth of invasive species like Eurasian water-milfoil, low water-milfoil forms modest patches in shallow areas. Its preference for fluctuating water levels also sets it apart from relatives that prefer consistently deep water.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Eurasian water-milfoil has more finely divided leaves than most of its native relatives, with leaflets that are thread-like and numerous.
Among New England's water-milfoils, broadleaf water-milfoil stands out for having distinctly broader surface leaves compared to most relatives like Eurasian water-milfoil.
Unlike its native milfoil cousins that stay mostly submerged, parrot's feather boldly emerges above water with bright green foliage.
Among New England's water-milfoils, Slender Water-milfoil lives up to its name with the most delicate, thread-like leaf divisions.
Unlike the aggressive Eurasian water-milfoil which forms dense mats, alternate water-milfoil grows in looser colonies and has its distinctive alternately-arranged flowers rather than whorled ones.
Siberian water-milfoil differs from other milfoils by its relatively short flower spikes and less aggressive spreading habit compared to invasive species like Eurasian water-milfoil.
Unlike the invasive Eurasian water-milfoil which has leaves scattered along the stem, whorled water-milfoil has its distinctive whorled leaf arrangement.
